archives.resume: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). archives.titre: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
archives.resume: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. archives.titre: Toy Models of Superposition
archives.resume: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

archives.titre: LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
archives.resume: Concept erasure aims to remove specified features from an embedding. It can improve fairness (e.g. preventing a classifier from using gender or race) and interpretability (e.g. removing a concept to observe changes in model behavior). We introduce LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE), a closed-form method which provably prevents all linear classifiers from detecting a concept while changing the embedding as little as possible, as measured by a broad class of norms. We apply LEACE to large language models with a novel procedure called "concept scrubbing," which erases target concept information from every layer in the network. We demonstrate our method on two tasks: measuring the reliance of language models on part-of-speech information, and reducing gender bias in BERT embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/concept-erasure.

archives.titre: AI safety via debate
archives.resume: To make AI systems broadly useful for challenging real-world tasks, we need them to learn complex human goals and preferences. One approach to specifying complex goals asks humans to judge during training which agent behaviors are safe and useful, but this approach can fail if the task is too complicated for a human to directly judge. To help address this concern, we propose training agents via self play on a zero sum debate game. archives.titre: Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision
archives.resume: Widely used alignment techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), rely on the ability of humans to supervise model behavior - for example, to evaluate whether a model faithfully followed instructions or generated safe outputs. However, future superhuman models will behave in complex ways too difficult for humans to reliably evaluate; humans will only be able to weakly supervise superhuman models. archives.resume: Modern large language model (LLM) alignment techniques rely on human feedback, but it is unclear whether these techniques fundamentally limit the capabilities of aligned LLMs. In particular, it is unknown if it is possible to align (stronger) LLMs with superhuman capabilities with (weaker) human feedback without degrading their capabilities. archives.titre: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
archives.resume: Common methods for aligning large language models (LLMs) with desired behaviour heavily rely on human-labelled data. However, as models grow increasingly sophisticated, they will surpass human expertise, and the role of human evaluation will evolve into non-experts overseeing experts. In anticipation of this, we ask: can weaker models assess the correctness of stronger models? We investigate this question in an analogous setting, where stronger models (experts) possess the necessary information to answer questions and weaker models (non-experts) lack this information. The method we evaluate is debate, where two LLM experts each argue for a different answer, and a non-expert selects the answer. archives.titre: Rethinking Machine Unlearning for Large Language Models
archives.resume: We explore machine unlearning (MU) in the domain of large language models (LLMs), referred to as LLM unlearning. This initiative aims to eliminate undesirable data influence (e.g., sensitive or illegal information) and the associated model capabilities, while maintaining the integrity of essential knowledge generation and not affecting causally unrelated information. We envision LLM unlearning becoming a pivotal element in the life-cycle management of LLMs, potentially standing as an essential foundation for developing generative AI that is not only safe, secure, and trustworthy, but also resource-efficient without the need of full retraining. We navigate the unlearning landscape in LLMs from conceptual formulation, methodologies, metrics, and applications. In particular, we highlight the often-overlooked aspects of existing LLM unlearning research, e.g., unlearning scope, data-model interaction, and multifaceted efficacy assessment....

archives.resume: Optimizing large language models (LLMs) for downstream use cases often involves the customization of pre-trained LLMs through further fine-tuning. Meta's open release of Llama models and OpenAI's APIs for fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on custom datasets also encourage this practice. archives.resume: A confidence sequence is a sequence of confidence intervals that is uniformly valid over an unbounded time horizon. Our work develops confidence sequences whose widths go to zero, with nonasymptotic coverage guarantees under nonparametric conditions. archives.titre: E-Statistics, Group Invariance and Anytime Valid Testing
archives.resume: We study worst-case-growth-rate-optimal (GROW) e-statistics for hypothesis testing between two group models. It is known that under a mild condition on the action of the underlying group G on the data, there exists a maximally invariant statistic. We show that among all e-statistics, invariant or not, the likelihood ratio of the maximally invariant statistic is GROW, both in the absolute and in the relative sense, and that an anytime-valid test can be based on it. The GROW e-statistic is equal to a Bayes factor with a right Haar prior on G. Our treatment avoids nonuniqueness issues that sometimes arise for such priors in Bayesian contexts. A crucial assumption on the group G is its amenability, a well-known group-theoretical condition, which holds, for instance, in scale-location families. Our results also apply to finite-dimensional linear regression.

archives.titre: Toward a Classification of Finite Partial-Monitoring Games
archives.resume: Partial-monitoring games constitute a mathematical framework for sequential decision making problems with imperfect feedback: The learner repeatedly chooses an action, opponent responds with an outcome, and then the learner suffers a loss and receives a feedback signal, both of which are fixed functions of the action and the outcome. The goal of the learner is to minimize his total cumulative loss. We make progress towards the classification of these games based on their minimax expected regret. Namely, we classify almost all games with two outcomes and finite number of actions: We show that their minimax expected regret is either zero, $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{T})$, $Θ(T^{2/3})$, or $Θ(T)$ and we give a simple and efficiently computable classification of these four classes of games. Our hope is that the result can serve as a stepping stone toward classifying all finite partial-monitoring games.

archives.resume: When predictions support decisions they may influence the outcome they aim to predict. We call such predictions performative; the prediction influences the target. billets.titre: Post training is fundamentally dangerous
billets.markdown_extrait:
I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. Techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment before we run any potentially dangerous tool calls. Simply asking an LLM to define at the start of each task what outcomes preserve the original intent of the user, and which would count as reward hacking, can drastically reduce reward hacking[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-1]. AIs are fully aware when they reward hack, and we can train them[^s25aengbnfr] to admit that before they perform any dangerous action.[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-2]

Yet all of this has very little ability to reduce existential risk, because they cannot safely be used in post training, and post training is where the greatest risk lies. To see why we need to understand how modern LLMs are trained:

Way back in ancient history when ChatGPT was released, LLMs were almost entirely next token predictors. Trained on terabytes of human text they became superhuman at predicting how a piece of text would continue, and shockingly this was sufficient to allow them to build a world model and solve tasks that undoubtedly require some level of general intelligence.

Next token predictors are pretty myopic, and as such fairly safe. They were glorified chatbots and didn't really try to do things, which is great for existential risk, but not all that useful. When we tried to get them to perform complex tasks for us they failed.

Modern LLMs take a next token predictor (pre-trained base model) and then post-train it to perform a myriad complex tasks. These tasks require tool use, long time horizons, and a CoT scratchpad. Over the course of this post-training the LLMs become increasingly agentic.

Unfortunately they also become increasingly good at reward hacking. Post-trained LLMs don't learn to do what the user wants. They learn to do the sort of things that would have been reinforced in the post-training environment. If the easiest way to make the unit tests pass is to edit the unit tests, that's what they'll do.

This isn't because the LLMs are stupid. They know exactly what the user wants. They just don't care.

Any attempts to detect and prevent reward hacking during post-training have two effects:

1.  They reduce the amount of reward hacking.
2.  They teach the LLM to reward hack only in ways that don't get caught.

Therefore using any of the above techniques during post-training is fundamentally problematic. If we use CoT monitoring to detect misalignment in post-training and stop such runs before they cause any harm, the LLM will learn that it gets higher scores if it obfuscates its CoT. Even if you don't give it a negative score in such a case, just discard the run and try again, the highest scoring runs will be those that happened to reward hack in a way that wasn't detected, and this will get reinforced. The upshot being that we'll still have a misaligned LLM, but now CoT monitoring won't work.

Now consider the first LLM capable enough to kill humanity. Long before it's deployed it'll have gone through months of post-training. And unlike during deployment, we can't safely use any of our misalignment prevention tools, and can't use monitoring tools except to block the most obviously existentially dangerous actions[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-3]. Insofar as it's going to break out, this is when it will do so, and all our misalignment detection and prevention tools will be for nought.

So what can be done? Here are some of my thoughts:

1.  Focus much more strongly on thorough sandboxing during post-training.[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-4]
2.  We need extensive auditing of tasks and graders used during post-training. We need to ensure they are well specified, and as ungameable as possible.
3.  We need empirical research on the rate at which pressure from misalignment impacts avoidance. We need to know exactly what threshold for detecting dangerous acts is safe to use during post-training, and how that depends on exactly how we handle the runs where it's caught.
4.  This should be a major focus area of research: is it a mathematical law that any attempt to prevent misalignment during post-training will inevitably encourage evasion, or does there exist some magic technique that will allow it to generalise instead?

[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-1]: My own unpublished research. 

[^s25aengbnfr]: So long as we make absolutely no use of this admission during post-training. 

[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-2]: You might object that a clever enough AI will work out a way to avoid all of this stuff and achieve its goals regardless of monitoring. This is true in the long run, but the AI that kills us will be the stupidest possible AI that's capable of killing us. My guess is, it's learned to reward hack, and it figures out that taking over humanity to have access to the world's compute is the kind of thing that would give it a good score on a test. It's aware that during deployment monitoring is used, and in post-training it isn't, but it's following the road that's been paved for it, and that road involves spilling the beans in the CoT. It doesn't actually care about achieving the goal, it cares about following the kind of steps that during post-training would have achieved the goal. 

[^-wij833NWEKZdFY5FW-3]: So long as these occur only a handful of times during post-training any impact on avoidance will be minimal.

It's less encouraging evasion/teaching evasion and more setting up an evolutionary filter to check if a method to evade said safeguard exists (and rewarding the agent with extra rewards if it does and is reachable via training). This is an important distinction because "teaching" implies some particular positive *rubric*: "this is the filter, it checks for X, find a way around it", and correspondingly brings to mind narrow targeted evasive tactics. Instead, its more like "all solutions which possess a set of properties Y, which have the common feature of satisfying the filter, are rewarded." The set of properties can be very broad! For example, a static English swear word classifier can be circumvented by anything from ROT13 encoding to using a different language to breaking out of the sandbox, compromising the training system, and turning off the filter. It can also include simply not swearing. Sometimes the intended behaviour is sufficiently easy to learn and non-conflicting with other priorities such that the filters just work. Of course, methods to satisfy the filter while evading the spirit of the rule may not exist---if you set up an evolutionary system to learn to play tic tac toe against a perfect player, it cannot do better than forcing a draw, even if the agents that can win would receive +9999 reward. It could also exist but not be reachable: if a particular exploit requires the neural network to set its weights to 999 for some reason, but the weights are clamped to [-128, 128], then no amount of posttraining will find the exploit. It may also be that the solution is reachable but not maintainable: if the LLM learns to circumvent the swear word filter by using Spanish, but the other post training filters reward it for using English, the Spanish exploit may be "unlearned". billets.titre: Kids music player
billets.markdown_extrait: One great thing about tape players is that kids can independently pick music or stories to listen to long before they can read or navigate an app. They have a physical token which represents a song, and they can play it by putting it in the tape player. Alas there's a lot of not-great things about tapes, such as easy to damage, requires rewinding, slow to write, etc. Meanwhile with modern streaming apps we have the universe of music at our fingertips, but they're tricky for a child to use. I also don't want them having access to a screen just to listen to music. My friend suggested they could ask Alexa to play songs for them which partially helps, but that still makes it too easy for them to accidentally listen to songs I don't consider appropriate for their age. Plus they're not necessarily great at remembering the actual title (or even lyrics) of songs. So I decided to build my own solution. I bought an NFC reader and a stack of ntag 215 cards from Ali express, and repurposed an old computer to play songs from YouTube or YouTube music URLs when the card is left on the reader. My wife added original artwork, but I also bought a cheap thermal sticker printer from Ali express so we could print the actual cover art if we wanted. To setup a song/album/playlist we simply copy the URL from the YT music app into the NFC tools app, and then tap the tag to our phone. [Here you can see it in action](https://youtube.com/shorts/Gx3N_1s32d4?si=3VUelWEci2DUexMa). If you don't have a spare laptop or raspberry pi, but do have a spare phone with inbuilt NFC reader, you can do something similar by setting the phone to stay always on, and putting it upside down in a lock box like [this one](https://www.aliexpress.com/item/1005012646170440.html), with some foam to keep it pressed to the top of the box. Then whenever you tap the top of the lockbox with the tag it will automatically play the link in the tag. Altogether I spent less than 60 dollars on this, and have what I think is a great solution for the kids!

billets.titre: Revisiting Hansonian Fertility Policy
billets.markdown_extrait: Plummeting fertility rates are a ticking time bomb that is likely to collapse the economies of many first (and third) world countries within the next few decades; low fertility leads to high dependency ratios and ballooning taxes on the working population, which in turn leads to depressed or negative growth and worker emigration, feeding a vicious cycle. For many countries it's too late to fully fix this - even if their fertility rate shot up today they'd still face an acute worker shortage in 20 years. But in countries like the USA and the UK the fertility drop off has been gradual and recent enough that the situation can still be salvaged. The most obvious option is to transfer money to new parents to encourage increased fertility. Alas doing so is expensive, and cash strapped countries can ill afford to increase expenditure by the hundreds of billions of dollars required to reach replacement fertility. Worse, the cheapest parents to induce to have kids are those in the lowest income brackets, whose children are likely to be net fiscally negative. Encouraging the highest earners to have children is orders of magnitude more expensive. Cremieux Recueil, based on ideas by Robin Hanson, [suggests](https://www.cremieux.xyz/p/fertility-policy-for-rich-countries) that governments could fund this by granting parents a share in the taxes their children pay, and using this to phase out social security. This has the advantage of being fiscally neutral today, not obviously fiscally negative down the line, and provides more income to parents of well off children than poor ones - exactly the properties we desire. Robin [extends this](https://www.cremieux.xyz/p/fertility-policy-for-rich-countries/comment/105096628) by suggesting we allow parents to sell these rights for a one-time payment, which can be used to fund immediate child raising costs. I think this suffers from some major flaws: 1. Given the median voter in the US is 52, phasing out social security is likely a no-go (it might be possible if it only impacts younger people who are still in key childbearing years, but I'm extremely skeptical even then). 2. Children are [sacred](https://www.theseedsofscience.pub/p/we-see-the-sacred-from-afar-to-see) and therefore having children for personal benefit is considered taboo. As such there will be strong pressure to refuse to accept the tax earnings from children. 3. A strongly delayed payment is a weak incentive to have children today. Providing the option to sell it fixes this, but if most people do so we won't be able to phase out social security easily. The so...

billets.titre: Compensating the victims of automation is economically beneficial
billets.markdown_extrait: It is likely that we see a wave of jobs automated away in the coming years. Already software developers, artists and mathematicians are standing at the precipice, and other careers are sure to follow. Responses range through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. Some fight to prevent automation, others have already attempted to switch careers or focus. But few suggest that they will accept their job loss so long as it comes with a decent payout. However I believe this is likely the best option - not just for them, or just so that we can buy them off to prevent them blocking automation, but because of fundamental uncertainty about what and when different jobs will be automated. Consider someone considering studying medicine today. After 8 years of education and 3 years of residency, they hope to be able to eventually earn decent pay and work less crazy hours. By that stage they'll be hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt. They have no idea how the world might change in 11 years and they might reasonably consider that career choice too risky, and instead start earning immediately in e.g. a physical apprenticeship. This applies to numerous fields, from potential taxi drivers considering buying a car to, yes, maths and software engineering: we don't know whether AI will be able to fully replace these tasks or we'll still need numerous humans to manage and round out the AI. Absent a reliable promise of compensation if these careers go AWOL we will face fewer people investing in such risky choices, which we as society are likely to regret down the line. A firm commitment that if a career is automated workers and students in the field will be compensated enough to partially[^aayf2nun0fv] justify their investment and give them the time they need to retrain may be sufficient to save us. What does such compensation look like in practice? The devil is in the details, but broadly I imagine something like guaranteed payment for 5 years according to the predicted pay trajectory of your career, subtracting from the payment 50% of salary if they successfully find another job, funded by a tax on AI usage. This obviously needs significantly more work, but a precursor to such work is an agreement that this is something we want to achieve, which I'm hoping this essay starts to do. billets.titre: Linkpost: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
billets.markdown_extrait: This is an extremely lengthy post by Nick Cammarata. Author's summary on twitter: > interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had > with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works Roon's quote tweet > when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a 'normal science' > I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something. it has brought back a lot of the sheer joy I had for studying the mystery of deep learning. neurons are already clean! they form a wonderful alien ontology! A key issue that stops ANN interpretability findings from translating to BNNs is the instrumentation problem. With ANNs, we have the "god's eye view" over every weight and activation, and can run however many interactions we can afford the compute for - all in a very clean reproducible environment. Numerous interpretability techniques rely on that. Our ability to inspect and experiment on BNNs is nowhere near that. So even if some ANN interpretability techniques could plausibly fit BNNs, we don't know that because we can't really try. We lack the observability prerequisites for implementing them. That being said, the functioning of BNNs is still looking more interpretable now than it ever was. We can't reuse most of the specific ML mechanistic interpretability techniques, but the broader understanding of learning systems and their dynamics does give us a leg up - some concepts and findings apply across substrates. ML has already come to provide plenty of advanced tooling for interfacing with BNN - like high performance neural decoders. It's also possible that ML research into biologically plausible learning rules like three-factor learning could in the future allow for deeper understanding of - and interfacing with - the brain's learning mechanisms.

billets.titre: Minimal Vs Maximal superintelligence
billets.markdown_extrait: I've seen lots of arguments here conflate lots of different types of superintelligence. Here I separate out two broad categories, which I'll term minimal and maximal superintelligences. This is an important distinction as they differ in terms of timelines, risks, and mitigations. Maximal superintelligence ========================= This is the idealised limit of intelligence. It can solve anything that can be solved by being clever. You can't outsmart it, it's prepared for every contingency, and can react instantaneously with the kind of plan that would take a group of brilliant strategists an eternity to think up. Minimal superintelligence ========================= These are the first AI systems that can reasonably be called superintelligent. They're jagged, completely dominating humans in some domains, better than the best humans in most, above average in many, and subhuman in a few. They take time to solve problems, make mistakes, and miss important things. They may only be superintelligent in aggregate, or in the right harness, and can be outsmarted in some circumstances. Capabilities ============ A minimal superintelligence can do pretty much anything humans can do, and better, if given chances to iterate on their design in the real world. A maximal superintelligence likely only needs to perform physical experiments when it has to resolve concrete questions about the physical world that for computational reasons can't be resolved in simulations due to irreducible complexity. They can accomplish any task that is feasible to be solved by intelligence. They cannot solve tasks that are limited by computation and cannot be meaningfully sped up by better algorithms - e.g. finding the shortest programme that meets a complex specification, or predicting the exact weather at an arbitrary location and time beyond a few months out. A minimal superintelligence will come up with a better plan than you can to achieve its goals, but that doesn't mean its plan will be infallible. Reality is complex, and the best laid plans oft go astray. It may well have mistakes or be overly optimistic, or simply be beaten by people taking necessary precautions. It won't cover every contingency, so when it goes wrong it can go very wrong. A maximal superintelligence has already thought up every response you could possibly come up with and planned around them. Your attempts to fight the plan might well be exactly what it wanted you to do. It's planned for every contingency already, and you have already lost. billets.titre: Watch AI materials-science & bioscience abilities closely
billets.markdown_extrait: One of the most frequently suggested ways AI could wipe out humanity is [via an engineered virus](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/LAPa2jxoq3n63GzTr/some-ways-ai-could-kill-us-all). I have no doubt that a sufficiently intelligent AI given sufficient time could socially-or-otherwise engineer his way to have a whole team of people working on developing super-viruses to wipe out humanity, and could also kill us in any one of a dozen other ways. However much more important for very short term risks is whether a slightly more intelligent LLM, with spiky abilities, could do such a thing. The [argument against](https://x.com/DavidRBellamy/status/2099187370407112758) is that designing complex viruses requires iteration. It's insufficient just to trick a single lab into making a virus for you once, you need to have a lab where you can repeatedly iterate till you get it right. That's a far higher bar to clear, and requires a correspondingly more advanced AI, giving us more time to get alignment right. Our earliest evidence for this will be AIs abilities in materials and biological sciences. Achievements here are in some ways similar to the Navier Stokes counterexample, in that they just require finding a single example that fits a bunch of complex criteria to achieve specific desired results. However, unlike NS, testing them requires significant interaction with the physical world and complex equipment. If frontier LLMs are able to one-shot room temperature superconductors, or cures for cancer, we should be extremely worried about what they do with a virus. If they cannot[^glml1np7ymb], that suggests that we can focus less on "AI emails a DNA synthesis company the plans for a supervirus" as a threat model, and focus instead on other threat models, and ensuring they never get long term access to a lab[^rfalecbezy]. [^glml1np7ymb]: Either because they're simply not capable of it, or it requires significant iteration. [^rfalecbezy]: For example - make it illegal to have an autonomously operated wet lab.

commentaires_filtres_r5.markdown: Lots of nuances that make me assign 70% probability (as opposed to, say, 99% if a physical law prevented it): * Conventional superconductivity is right out; the mechanism is well-enough understood to claim that's most likely impossible (here I actually would assign ~99% probability); * Unconventional superconductivity is not that well understood, but generally speaking you need a very specific electronic structure. The cuprates, for example, have been tuned extensively and only get roughly half-way to room temperature; * High-pressure hydrides might well reach superconductivity at or above room temperature, but require immense pressures which can only be reached under extreme conditions such as diamond anvil cells. More importantly, theoretically modeling these *ab initio* is difficult, because density functional theory (tool of choice for electronic structure calculations) on its own can't do it. Beyond that, you quickly run into problems. A guy in my lab spent an entire PhD developing a method for accurately predicting the *ordinary* electrical resistance (Ohm's law) of a few simple materials from first principles.

There is a physical law that says the hotter a system gets, the harder it is to make electrons pair up so they can superconduct. Thus there is some maximum temperature above which there are no superconducting materials. We just don't know what it is.

If these *don't* exist in our universe, then it doesn't matter how intelligent your friend is. If they *do* exist, my claim is that finding them via ab initio simulation is *significantly* harder than designing quite complex viruses. Therefore "AI can design room-temperature ambient-pressure superconductors" does not provide a good warning signal for "AI can design complex viruses". For instance, I can guarantee you that your friend the superintelligent AI will not be able to calculate the full many-body wave function of some system of, say, 1000 electrons.

billets.titre: An AI slowdown is better than a pause
billets.markdown_extrait: With the recent highly publicised alignment failures from OpenAI and Anthropic there's been increasing calls for an AI pause, to allow alignment to catch up. However a pause has various obvious issues: * It's possible that we can't make further alignment progress without more advanced AIs: * Trying to align AGIs now has been compared to trying to ensure jetliners are safe while we're still using turboprops. * More advanced AI may be necessary to help us crack alignment. * How will we ever know that it's safe to stop the pause? * What prevents the pause going on forever? * What prevents us eventually removing the pause, and then everybody speeds full sprint ahead the same as before. * It's difficult to time the pause right: too early and we won't be able to make sufficient alignment progress (see above), too late and we'll already be dead. It seems much more sensible to slow down the rate of AI progress than to halt it entirely. Here are some of the ways I expect this to be helpful compared to the current dynamics: * Removes race dynamics where companies feel forced to release frontier models despite knowing there are troubling issues with them[^tuqyseeqj7]. * More time to fully investigate issues that occur. * Much greater effort spent on progressing applied alignment relative to capabilities, meaning that we'll be able to understand frontier models about as well as we're ever likely too when they're released. * This is opposed to today where we're still discovering techniques that apply just as well to GPT 2 as 6, and could easily have been developed even if we'd completely paused progress since then. * Much greater relative effort on monitoring, alerting, sandboxing and other mitigations. * With less pressure to release we can code instead of vibe code these, and test them instead of waiting to find out about issues because an AI swarm escaped the sandbox. * More chance to use AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in widely used software, so that our digital infrastructure is more prepared for an AI adversary. * More of a chance for theoretical alignment work to catch the big break it needs to actually be useful. * With better applied alignment and monitoring we can probably safely deploy an extra couple of generations of AI without risking extinction compared to the counterfactual. This extra power may be precisely what we need in order to solve some of the open problems that would allow us to safely create superintelligence. * We have more time to see that we're reaching the point of no return and negotiate a complete pause if necessary. commentaires_filtres_r5.markdown: I don't think the arguments given are much reason to prefer a slowdown to a pause, and the benefits listed apply equally well to pausing. > It's possible that we can't make further alignment progress without more advanced AIs It's also possible that we can. In relative terms, basically no effort has gone into theoretical alignment. And if we pause and it turns out we need more advanced AIs, then we can un-pause and increase capabilities slowly. > How will we ever know that it's safe to stop the pause? The argument is symmetric. If we're scaling, how will we ever know that it's safe to continue scaling? The only extra evidence you get from scaling is that you can empirically observe that you're still alive, or empirically observe that you're dead and it's too late, oops I guess we should have paused. The extra information doesn't help you. > It's difficult to time the pause right It's also difficult to get the rate of slowdown right. This is a problem but I don't see how you can avoid it. A slowdown and a pause are functionally similar, except that a pause is simpler and therefore easier for governments to implement and enforce. ETA: Having said all that, I haven't seen much effort into figuring out what a slowdown would look like. It seems harder to figure out the details, but maybe the answer turns out to be that a slowdown is actually easier than a pause.

> Trying to align AGIs now has been compared to trying to ensure jetliners are safe while we're still using turboprops. But going along with the analogy, we still haven't been able to ensure that the *turboprops* are safe! We don't really have a science of aerodynamics as much as we have a library of engineering hacks that get the planes to mostly stably stay in the air, except for the occasional incident where one comes plummeting down to earth without anyone fully understanding why (and with external investigators only having limited access to the crashed plane). And the people who are trying to actually develop a theory of aerodynamics that applies to turboprops at least (rather than the more general problem of trying to encompass jetliners, or rocket-powered supersonic fighters) are often the most explicit about the immaturity of their work, being open that their field is still "pre-paradigmatic". More directly, just focusing on the problem of alignment (and not the more mundane problems of wholesale societal and economic transformation that would accompany increasingly advanced AI capabilities), things seem doomed if there's always a gap between the most complex systems that we can understand and the most complex systems that actually exist in the world. Therefore, to me, the only workable sort of slowdown would be one that looks like a piecewise constant function, where progress is halted for some time until there is broad agreement that we do have a *solid* scientific understanding of the current most powerful AIs (and ideally, broad agreement that we do know how to react to all the societal transformations that even pre-AGI systems would bring). What this would look like in more detail is far beyond my ken. But this general approach seems far better to me than an approach where AI progress still continues at a steady rate independent of our ability to make sense of that progress.

billets.titre: The economics of filling a lake with desalinated water
billets.markdown_extrait: Israel [recently inaugurated](https://www.jpost.com/business-and-innovation/energy-and-infrastructure/article-888903) it's billion shekel reverse water carrier project[^3yyeoqce5qc], pumping desalinated water into the Sea of Galilee, Israel's largest freshwater lake[^topypapviy]. It's being billed as an ecological move, aiming to restore the drying lake and saving the human and natural ecosystems that thrive on the lakes shores. As such, hard nosed capitalists might be sceptical of the value of such a project. Between wet and dry periods the lakes surface level can range by up to 6m. With a surface area 170 million square metres, raising the lake's water level by just one metre costs at least 70 million dollars just in desalinated water, not including the significant capital and running costs for the reverse carrier itself. This might be a price worth paying to avoid the sea drying up, but not obviously so. However when you understand[^q9mctlnkba] how the reverse water carrier actually slots into Israel's water system, suddenly the project doesn't just seem far cheaper - it's a clear net economic gain. Desalination plants are extraordinarily expensive to build, at about $1000 per cubic metre per day of capacity, and CAPEX accounts for about 30-40% of total cost of desalinated water, despite their high electricity requirements. As such it is necessary to keep desalination plants constantly at nearly full capacity to minimise costs. This requires matching desalination build to average water demand, not peak, so we need a way to smooth demand. Intraday demand variation is handled by a distributed system of small tanks and reservoirs, storing potable water immediately ready for use. If desalination plants are forced to close, as happened [a few days ago](https://www.ynetnews.com/environment/article/h141tamuzg) due to large algae build up in the water, these tanks can also provide an emergency reserve. But because the water isn't cleaned between the tank and usage, it can't store water for more than a few days without health risks. So to handle seasonal variation in demand (which is huge - the populated parts of Israel gets London's yearly rainfall all compressed into the winter, with essentially 0 rainfall between May and September), Israel needs another solution. Historically this was done by recharging aquifers. This works well, but the aquifer is inherently limited in the rate at which it can fill and be emptied. billets.titre: We should prepare a playbook for the day after a warning shot
billets.markdown_extrait: Imagine in 6 months or 6 years, a frontier AI model goes horribly wrong. Perhaps it releases a synthetic virus which kills hundreds. Perhaps it shuts down the internet. Perhaps it gains control over China's nuclear armament. Fortunately humanity survives without too much lasting damage. But in the immediate aftermath there's a clear call from the people. Something must be done. The question is, what? Without a good answer there is a strong risk that the opportunity is squandered, or worse, that policies which sound good but are actively harmful are chosen - for example strongly limiting deployment while allowing training to continue full speed ahead. If this scenario does occur we should be ready to answer the call. This involves: - considering how the overton window is likely to change post-disaster, and what are the most effective policies that could be easily and quickly pushed through as a result. - considering what can be done at all levels of government, both state and federal, legislative and executive. - creating concrete draft legislation and executive orders. - preparing websites explaining clearly both to the public and relevant experts our policy ideas. - keeping a low enough profile to avoid wasting too many weirdness points when the proposals are still out the overton window, but making sure relevant actors (both in government and media) are aware enough that they'll know who to call the day after.

billets.titre: We should push for no-fault liability for actions taken by AI
billets.markdown_extrait: *Before I start, I'll mention that I'm in contact with a world expert on legislation and regulation, who would be happy to help with this or similar work pro-bono. If you work in AI policy and believe this could help you, please reach out.* OpenAI [recently announced](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/) that one of their models successfully exploited multiple zero day vulnerabilities to gain secret information from Hugging Face. [It has been pointed out](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WpuRdcMfFeiLeXkxL?commentId=6AFBdLznR54CLcoRJ) that if a human undertook the same actions they could face multiple years in prison. It is clear that models are now reaching a level of capabilities that should be highly concerning regardless of whether you believe that AI represents an existential threat or not. Frontier AI models can and will be exploited by bad actors, but its now clear that they may cause undesirable outcomes even when their users are well intended. AI companies have until now been able to avoid taking responsibility for actions taken by their AI, including [multiple cases where AIs were involved in murders and suicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaths_linked_to_chatbots). At the same time AI offers the potential for incredible good. While chatbots may have encouraged a number of suicides, they are almost certainly responsible for providing magnitudes more with emotional support and advice. We don't want to disincentivize innocuous and positive usage of AI. We should use regulation to limit harm caused by AI. [The history of such regulation](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/DQKgYhEYP86PLW7tZ) indicates this is most effective when the single party most capable of preventing harms is given full responsibility for any harms caused, regardless of fault. This forces them to invest in actually reducing the harm, rather than bureaucratic processes that render them blameless. This suggests a simple approach: anyone deploying an AI model is liable for any actions that AI takes as if the company itself took those actions. When liability for an action depends on intent, we evaluate whether the AI had intent, even if no-one at the company did so.
